title: Paint your own blue pottery bowl
takeHome: A bowl or tile you painted yourself, fired and wrapped (or shipped if it needs a second firing day)
summary: Knead the quartz dough, shape a small piece, then paint a ready-dried bowl in cobalt and turquoise. Gentle, meditative, very messy hands.

steps.title: Chai and the secret
steps.text: Anjali shows you why blue pottery isn't clay, with a lump of quartz dough you can squish.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Press dough into a mould to make a small dish. It goes into the drying racks for another day.

steps.title: Sketch
steps.text: Pick a ready, dried bowl and sketch your design with a soft pencil. Flowers, birds or your own idea.

steps.title: Paint
steps.text: Paint with fine brushes in cobalt, turquoise and white. Wobbly lines are welcome here.

steps.title: Glaze and fire
steps.text: Watch the glazing, peek at the kiln, and collect your piece once it's fired and cooled.

wear: Old clothes or an apron (they lend one). Short sleeves help. Closed shoes near the kiln.
safety: The kiln gets very hot; stay behind the line and let the host handle all loading. Glazes and pigments aren't for skin or mouths, so wash hands before snacks. Kids under 10 should paint only.
gettingThere: About 15–20 minutes from the old city on Amer Road. Take an app auto or cab to the drop pin. Drivers may suggest a 'better' pottery place; politely say you've booked.

title: Hand-block print a stole in Sanganer
takeHome: A cotton stole or two napkins you printed, colour-fixed and ready to wear
summary: Stand at a long printing table in a real courtyard and learn the thump-lift-move rhythm with Sanganer's classic floral blocks.

steps.title: Meet the blocks
steps.text: Handle old and new wooden blocks and see how one is carved for each colour.

steps.title: Choose a design
steps.text: Pick 2 or 3 blocks: a border, a buti and a filler.

steps.title: Practice
steps.text: Print on scrap cloth first. Ramesh ji will fix your wrist angle; everyone needs it.

steps.title: Print your piece
steps.text: Print your stole: outline first, then fill colour, lining up the repeats by eye.

steps.title: Dry and fix
steps.text: Sun-dry and fix the colour while you have chai and look at the drying fields.

wear: Dark, washable clothes. Dye splashes happen. Tie long hair back.
safety: Pigments are mostly water-based but can stain and irritate; gloves are offered and you should use them if your skin is sensitive. Don't eat at the printing table.
gettingThere: Sanganer is about 30–40 minutes south of the old city, near the airport. An app cab is easiest. Share the host's pin, not 'Sanganer printing', or you may land at a big showroom.

title: Dabu mud-resist and indigo in Bagru
takeHome: An indigo-dyed dabu scarf with your own mud-resist print
summary: Mix the mud paste, press it on with a block, dust it with sawdust and dip into indigo. Slow, earthy, and a little bit magic when the green cloth turns blue.

steps.title: Mud kitchen
steps.text: See how dabu paste is made from mud, lime, natural gum and wheat husk.

steps.title: Print the resist
steps.text: Block-print the paste onto cotton and sprinkle sawdust so it sets.

steps.title: Dry
steps.text: Let it dry in the sun while Kamla ji shows you older dabu pieces.

steps.title: Indigo dip
steps.text: Dip the cloth in the indigo vat and watch it turn from green to blue in the air.

steps.title: Wash out
steps.text: Rinse off the mud and reveal the pattern. Your cloth is then dried for you to take home.

wear: Clothes you don't mind turning slightly blue, and sandals that can get muddy. A hat for the sun.
safety: Indigo vats can irritate skin and eyes, so wear the gloves provided and don't lean over the vat. Keep children with you near the dye pits. Drink water; it's an outdoor, sunny workshop.
gettingThere: Bagru is about 30–35 km west of Jaipur on the Ajmer road, roughly an hour by cab. Book a return cab or ask the driver to wait; app cabs are harder to find back from the village.

title: Tie and dye your own bandhani scarf
takeHome: A cotton bandhani scarf you tied and dyed, plus a tiny sample of fine dots tied by Shabnam ji
summary: In a family home above Johari Bazaar, learn to pinch and tie knots, dye your scarf in two colours, and pull the knots open to see the dots appear.

steps.title: Look closely
steps.text: Compare fine and coarse bandhani and learn to spot a printed copy.

steps.title: Mark
steps.text: Mark your design with washable colour; a simple circle or wave pattern works best.

steps.title: Tie
steps.text: Pinch and tie knots with thread. Your fingers will complain; Shabnam ji will laugh kindly.

steps.title: Dye
steps.text: Dip in the first colour, rinse, tie a few more, then dip in the second colour.

steps.title: Open
steps.text: Pull the knots open and watch the dots appear. Best moment of the day.

wear: Clothes you don't mind staining; an apron is provided. Short nails make tying easier.
safety: Dyes are hot and can stain skin for a day or two, so use gloves and tongs at the dye pots. Kids should stick to tying and opening.
gettingThere: Walk or take an auto to Johari Bazaar. Cars can't get close at busy hours, so get dropped at the main road and follow the host's pin into the lane (about 3 minutes on foot).
